# dsh-memory-tree
**Long-term memory for DeepSeek Harness — an AST-indexed, tiered SQLite brain that survives sessions
ong-term memory for DeepSeek Harness — an AST-indexed, tiered SQLite brain that survives sessions.**
English | 中文

Your agent forgets. A task ends, the context is gone, the compaction summary dies with the
session,

and a new task in the same project starts from zero. Notes you saved last month never
surface when a
new idea connects to them.
This plugin makes memory an **asset on disk** instead of a consumable in the context window:

- **captures** every user/assistant exchange in the background,
- **indexes** it as an AST tree of a

ddressable nodes with embeddings and soft similarity links,
- **recalls** relevant nodes before each

turn and injects one bounded `<memory-recall>` block,
- **tiers** the data into hot/warm/cold SQLit

e files so the active file never grows with age,
- and exposes `mem_recall`, `mem_store`, `mem_stats
`, `mem_dream`, `mem_rotate` as tools.
No external service. No native build. One directory you can copy, inspect, back up, or delete.

## Compatibility
Tested with DSH **0.2.1-rc.3** (bundled Node 24) on Windows and Linux CI, Node 22 and 24; Node ≥ 22.

5
for CLI use. The plugin has no native build and no runtime dependency tree of its own — it resolve

s
DSH's `@deepseek-ai/*` packages from the profile.

`package.json` declares `engines.dsh` (`^0.2.1-alpha.2`), and `npm run compat` in CI asserts the
ses
sion-format injection rules too, so a DSH rule change turns CI red instead of breaking an install.
DSH-side changes degrade capability by capability rather than all at once:
| What breaks | What happens |
| The host rejects the injected message (e.g. another source-kind change) | auto-recall is switched

off after that turn and logged; capture and the `mem_recall` tool keep working |
| `agent/pre-step`

is renamed or gone | auto-recall is off, everything else stays |
| `session/event` is gone | capture

is off, the tools and recall stay |
| The engine child process crashes | it restarts; the conversat

and recall stay |
| The engine child process crashes | it restarts; the conversation is unaffected |
`mem_stats` prints a `compat:` line showing normal, degraded or off.
## Why not just a vector store?
| Need | Flat chunk RAG | This project |

| Find similar text | ✅ | ✅ embeddings |
| Address a memory ("the optogenetics idea") | ❌ anonymous

chunks | ✅ unique AST paths |
| Surface a hit's section / siblings | ❌ | ✅ one-hop tree activation |
| Explain why something was recalled | ❌ one cosine number | ✅ six named score terms + audit rows |

| Bound the active database | ❌ grows forever | ✅ hot/warm/cold rotation |
| Work offline / no vend

or | depends | ✅ Ollama or a deterministic fake embedder |
| Be inspected by a human | depends | ✅ M
arkdown mirror beside SQLite |
Details and the failures that shaped the design: **docs/PRINCIPLES.md**.

## Measured behaviour

`node scripts/bench.mjs --sizes 1000,10000,30000` on this machine (Windows, Node 24, fake
embedder s
o the numbers measure storage + retrieval, not the network):
| nodes | DB size | recall p50 | recall p95 | rotation | hot file after rotation |

- ~5.4 KB per node (1024-dim vector ≈ 4 KB of it);
- the hot file only holds the retention window —

that is the point of tiering;
- rotation moves documents, not copies; `compact()` reclaims the freed

pages;
- real-world recall adds one embedding round trip; auto-recall is capped by `recall.timeoutM

s`
(1.5 s) and silently skipped when slow.
## Storage tiers
| Tier | File | Default age | Vectors | Recall weight |

| hot | `memory.db` | < 30 days | kept | 1.00 |
| warm | `memory-warm.db` | 30–180 days | kept | 0.9

0 |
| cold | `memory-cold.db` | > 180 days | kept (`dropColdVectors: true` to drop) | 0.78 |

Rotation runs on a timer (6 h), after startup, and on demand via `mem_rotate`. Whole documents
move

with their nodes and embeddings; nothing is deleted. Dropping cold vectors keeps the archive
keyword
-searchable at a fraction of the size.
Set `storage.tiered: false` for the old single-file behaviour.
